situation: Throughout this semester, I have been working with the Australian Glass & Window Association in a technical administration role where I am responsible for auditing glass & window thermal performance simulations submitted to the Window Energy and Rating Scheme (WERS). I am responsible for ensuring that simulations made in LBNL software: Therm, Window and Optics, are simulated in accordance to rules and regulations set by the AFRC (Australian Fenestration Registration Council) and the NFRC (National Fenestration Registration Council) through the analysis of cross-sectional models of window frame members and their relevant thermal behaviour. This year has brought a significant spike in the submission count for simulations, and has created a backlog of pending submissions that must be audited. This has created some urgency to work through submissions as quickly as possible to maintain a low submission count without sacrificing thoroughness and consistency.
task_action: My primary task was to increase my auditing efficiency for these thermal simulations without sacrificing the thoroughness that ensures all simulations are consistent. I began by optimising my auditing processes through the use of more adequate file management methods to make keeping track of my completed audits and quickly switching between different submissions much faster. I adjusted visual settings that made keeping track of my cursor and identifying errors easier, further increasing audit speed. I followed this with increasing the amount of communication between the Engineers I work with and myself, clarifying issues that I am uncertain on with them rather than taking the time to read through the large list of rules and standards. This allowed for me to reduce time wasted finding specific rules through making use of the resources around me to quickly refer to points in my relevant documents and their advice. This also assisted with increasing my understanding of the rules, reducing the amount I need to refer to any documents. I also began tracking my progress more thoroughly which went hand-in-hand with my file management processes, allowing myself and the Engineers I work with to update association members on wait times and create plans to manage progress through the backlog.
result: Through implementation of the above actions, I aimed to address the increased workload that came with the increased submissions effectively, ensuring that my auditing processes remained robust, efficient and in full compliance with all relevant standards.
pfr: When I first heard about the expected spike in submission counts, I felt a relatively significant amount of pressure. I am an auditor to relieve the workload relating to WERS off my Engineer co-workers. The urgency related to processing these submissions without sacrificing accuracy created a unique circumstance, as speed and thoroughness were critical to maintaining a good workload for all parties. Upon reflecting on these initial feelings, I have realised that my stress was primarily due to the fear of failing to prove that I am a good worker. I realised in the moment that although cutting corners to reduce the backlog was an easy option, it would impact my integrity, and it was my responsibility to ensure that I optimise my processes in order to show that I am thorough and that all products on the WERS database are accurate and correct. As I began developing my actions to address this issue, I grew more confidence as I received positive feedback regarding my accuracy and efficiency, which led to more confidence and in turn, more efficiency. This realisation was crucial in handling the situation correctly.
learning: From this experience, I have learned the importance of maintaining integrity as an Engineer, regardless of the pressures of timelines and good image. I learnt that handling issues in a constructive way is much more valuable than cutting corners. Continuous improvement in processes is essential with changing demands, complimenting this with greater communication skills allow for efficiency without sacrificing essential responsibilities Engineers have. Through these reflections, I have developed a better understanding of the importance relating to responsibility in Engineering. This experience has been extremely enlightening in the benefits of streamlining approaches without sacrificing quality.

situation: So far this semester, I have been required to complete multiple group projects worth significant weighting in terms of the total assessment percentage. They are critical to achieving a good result within the subject and test on a wide variety of skills including not only technical problem solving but also presentational and articulation-based skills.
task_action: Within the various groups I've worked in, it is crucial to split the workload effectively and balance the tasks based around each students' strengths and weaknesses. However, my groups have had students who are less motivated than others and they have found themselves failing to meet deadlines which causes the entire group to suffer. In such cases, the concept of accountability is extremely important. If this behavior is not called out it becomes increasingly difficult to 'play catchup' and it is therefore critical to have these difficult conversations about why there has been a lack of effort as soon as possible. In my case, our group needed to reach out to the slow-moving teammates and hold them accountable so we could submit the group-task before the due-date. If these group members had not been held accountable, it is likely the project would have failed to meet the deadline. Similarly, we held ourselves accountable for the outcome of the project as we made significant effort to ensure the project would be delivered on time - even if this included chasing others for their portion of the work.
result: The outcome of this accountability is that the projects have all been submitted on time with an equal contribution from each member. This has resulted in my teams all submitting project we are proud of and we have felt like overall they have been a success.
pfr: I have always felt strongly against group projects. The idea of others being responsible for part of my assessment submission is frightening as I have had bad experiences in the past where my work has suffered because of the lack of effort by others. It is difficult to be accountable for the actions of others, however, this skill is required within group tasks. It is always challenging having conversations about why someone hasn't made any effort for a project, however, once the conversation is had it is often a big relief as the group-member usually responds by apologizing and committing themselves to making progress on the task. I'm very grateful that this happened when I reached out to our group members - they responded well and took the initiative to complete the tasks quickly as they realized others were depending on them and they began to hold themselves accountable meaning that nobody needed to continue chasing them up for missing work. If they had responded differently in a more defensive manner, the situation would have been made far more difficult and would have elevated the stress levels of our members within our group. I think that we handled the situation well and this is supported by our high mark for the task.
learning: The experience has not changed my opinions of group work - I still believe it is far more challenging than individual work as you are balancing the efforts of multiple people and not only for yourself. However, it has taught me about how you can make yourself accountable when the performance of others is lacking. You can hold yourself accountable by ensuring that you have reached out to your teammates and check if they need help with anything. Maybe they are struggling to understand the requirements of a project, or maybe they do not follow the same working hours as you and they are simply waiting for the weekend to complete the project rather than everybody else who uses their time during the week. I think this is a valuable skill which will prove useful in future leadership positions where I may be required to manage people. You need to know how to be accountable for not only your own actions but also ensuring that you are supporting the people around you and providing them the tools for success so that they too can be accountable for themselves. If there is no accountability, things do not get done, and that's why it is essential to have this characteristic within a team environment. Although stressful at the time, I am grateful for this experience as it has taught me a skill which I may not have learnt before.

situation: Balancing school, work, and fun has been tough. As my semester went on, last year, things got even harder. This journey has been about more than just juggling my responsibilities; it's been a deep dive into knowing myself better, recognizing my strengths, and understanding my limits. It's shown me that facing life's challenges is possible and can even be an opportunity for growth. situation: during a recent group project for the design of concrete, the challenge of creating a new concept that would solve our issues with loading for a span of a concrete beam arose. situation: In my place of work, autonomous sailing vessel and the systems aboard it (navigation, communication, datum-collection, etc.) had to be prepared for launch with the minimum chance of failure or "hiccoughs" during its scheduled operation.
task_action: A digital list of checks that had been compiled earlier and made into an online form was gone-through by pairs of workers and items ticked off one at a time. Several changes had been made to the form so that tasks specific to one boat or another could be marked as "not applicable" on forms related to boats that did not have the related equipment. Unfortunately, some undocumented changes had been made to the form by members of the operations or software departments without the knowledge of the shop workers or shop management. These forms are initially stored and filled-out client-side.and are only updated on the server when the form is submitted. Software or coding limitations meant that forms could not be submitted until completely filled out.
result: Some of the undocumented changes, along with the limitations of the form software, IT infrastructure and form design meant that forms could not be completed and filled out for some boats, and checks had to be documented manually in the old-fashioned way after being transcribed from a half-completed form. This resulted in significant confusion and wasted some of everyone's time, including workers and management from both the workshop and other departments. Luckily the launch of the boats was not delayed, but it added potential risk of a no-go to an already fraught situation.
pfr: I feel that the use of online forms is an ingenious way of ensuring consistent and instantaneous distribution of information regarding the check status of vessels within the company. However, its implementation both technically and within the communication infrastructure of the company leaves something to be desired. The issues arise from a combination of ambiguity as to the accountability of individuals for certain tasks and a lack of conscious effort to incorporate the forms and their continual updating into the existing communication infrastructure of the company. For example, the individuals filling out the forms are personally accountable for performing the checks and must sign their names on the form. This is a good thing, and ensures that if something goes wrong, the team knows who to ask about the state of the equipment before the incident in order to determine if the failure was a technical one or a failure of procedure allowing human error to be introduced. This responsibility does not appear to extend to the people who are directly making the form webpage, who have no direct contact with the boats. This means changes are made to the form that may betray slight misunderstandings or lack of understanding about the systems aboard the vessels, and which make the forms impossible to fill out completely and submit, causing delays. In addition, nobody initially knows who made the changes and on whose instruction they were made, so it is additionally difficult to rectify the problem. I feel more could be done to improve the fitness-for-purpose of the form software used for pre-operation checks, to facilitate better communication between those making the forms and those filling them out, and to extend personal accountability to those making changes to the forms so that changes may be documented and problems fixed more quickly.
learning: Several changes could be made to improve the pre-operation check form situation and reduce the likelihood of further issues. Firstly a very short meeting between workshop and software management to outline the issue and discuss possible fixes to the issues with submission and form editing would be helpful. Forms should be stored server-side and updated live as individual points are ticked. The "submission" button should be little more than a mark of completion that temporarily locks editing of the form. Secondly, a series of three or four short, half-hour meetings between the workshop manager and the lead programmer for the forms webpage should be arranged over the following week. This would allow the programmer time to visit the vessel and see the equipment for which he is adding form items and so that the workshop manager can help him arrive at a list and form structure that best reflects the needs of the workshop and operations teams. It would also allow the workshop manager to visit the programmer during his development process to collaborate and suggest changes to the form as it is being finalised. Similar meetings should be arranged in the week preceding the introduction of any significant changes to the form or its contents. Secondly, changes to the forms should be documented and numbered as with a more formal software development process. Updates should also be signed and dated. This would help ensure that any changes made are not simply ad-hoc additions made by the software team without checking with operations or the workshop and are instead made with purpose and following approval by management of all parties. Thirdly, a hard-copy backup for these forms should be devised so that in the event of a software issue, the checks can still be made and documented without immediate delay, to be transcribed into the digital archive later when time is not so short.

topic: The transferable skill I will be focusing on is transparency, accountability and collaboration in a team operation within the context of the Rube Goldberg Machine project.
situation: We as a team needed to start working on our individual Rube Goldberg Machine components.
task_action: We set a hard deadline for when we wanted all the machines and individual component videos to be completed (21st of October) and expected each team member to hold themselves accountable and deliver what was expected of them in a timely manner. We outlined a few expectations beforehand, such as that we wanted the videos to be filmed solely in landscape mode to make the final video more cohesive and that the footage should be relatively high quality. Members of the group also discussed with each other how they were planning on conducting the transitions between each element. For example, two members were using water bottles as a transition device, and had a conversation about what brand they were planning on using to make it as cohesive as possible. Throughout the week, team members sent videos of their machines into our group chat and uploaded them in the shared Google Drive for easier access. We also held team members who seemed to be lagging behind accountable by asking them where they were at with their machine and assessing to see if they needed any help by encouraging collaboration. Furthermore, we were all transparent with any issues we were having or any problems that could implicate the timely delivery of our components. For example, some team members had assessment tasks from other subjects that they were prioritizing which we all understood would take more leeway.
result: The result were 5 videos of every team member's two components that could be combined into a final video achieved through consistently holding people accountable.
pfr: It was initially an intimidating task for us as we were worried about being too assertive or too forthcoming when talking to team members and holding them accountable for not delivering work on time. For example, we have a team member who has not handed in any assessment task all semester and has barely contributed to the overall project. We weren't sure if he was going to actually produce a final video that we could use, so we held him accountable by reaching out to him and asking him where he was at and if he thought completing the project was feasible. He was transparent with us, and told us that he didn't think he could, but failed to provide a legitimate reason. We then communicated and collaborated with the team to remove him from the group as we didn't want to impede our own progress. Thus, we only had 5 RGM videos produced instead of the 6. But, we were able to exercise effective accountability over specific team members in a way that seemed reasonable.
learning: By consistently holding team members accountable throughout the process of developing our final video, we were able to learn how to be properly assertive, communicative and how to prioritize the team's best interest. It was important for us to be confrontational and transparent with how we all felt in regards to the lack of contribution from certain team members to move forward and be successful.

situation: Reflecting upon my time and resource management through this past semester, I notice that this had become a lacking skill of mine during the start of my study at Macquarie. So far I am in my second semester of studies at Macquarie, and whilst I believe I started my studies very excited and optimistic, university life has definitely given me a wakeup call. As since, beginning I’ve had to face many problems of varying types. Eventually through trial and error and help from my peers I have been able to solve these problems by, beginning to adjust my attitude and habits to further aid my future life as a student and eventually an engineer.
task_action: Undergoing attempts to improve my time and resource management, I have attempted to use several methods such as, to-do listing suggested by my ENG1050 tutor, prioritising tasks, improving my organisation, removing unnecessary distractions and improving my overall health. Thusly I have explored all of these options and created a subsequent approach to my time and resource management.
result: The approach I have now devised is to use to-do listing, prioritising tasks, removing unnecessary distractions and improving my overall health. By creating to-do listings, I am now able to layout all future tasks for each and the subsequent order in which I must complete each task, indirectly creating a prioritised order of tasks. Hence this is aided by removing unnecessary distractions from my workstation, by moving my workstation to a quieter room in the house and placing my mobile phone in a separate room whilst I am studying. Another addition is improving my overall health, lately I have been falling ill a lot due to unnecessary stress and not keeping a regular sleep schedule and/or not eating properly. I have now begun to prioritize improving these items, as pushing myself to the breaking point not healthy.
pfr: I was first made aware that my time and resources management needed work after my first semester at Macquarie university. I first noticed that due to my poor time and resource management my social life, and my activities such as rock climbing outside university were severally lacking and I had not been able to work on either for a while. Hence during the break, I took time to reflect on this and I concluded that this was not a healthy or sustainable approach to my university life, and I need to take a more balanced approach to my studies. I believe reality has reflected these assumptions very well as during the first semester I got injured during rock climbing many times as I was not paying attention to my health properly and I became disconnected with my friends, but once I began implementing these changes, I noticed considerable improvements to my health and attitude. With this knowledge in my future studies, I plan to implement similar strategies to balance my life to excel in all aspects.
learning: Through these experiences I have learned that maintaining a balanced life is crucial as, this allows me to consistently apply myself at a balanced rate. I have also realised that to make sure study is effective there are certain protocols you can take in to create an effective study environment and avoid burnout. Hence by approaching my latest studies using a more balanced method with effective strategies, I have been able to have a much healthier approach to my university study. Now I am also able to enjoy my social life and continue climbing whilst still staying on top of all of my studies. Although one other aspect I have realised is that I must add some flexibility to this strategy as some unforeseen events can come and effect this approach severally.

topic: The transferable skills I will be reflecting on are “Test, verification, validation, and certification” and “The innovation process” and how these relate to the engineering process.
situation: Following up on the first 5 weeks of ENG1050, from week 6 to week 11 as part of team C15 we have had the massive task of innovating and validating our RGM design. As the next step in our design process, we had to finalise our preliminary designs and began constructing our RGM. We had to overcome reliability issues across all of our events implementing the “test, verification, validation, and certification” processes to finalise these events.
task_action: For the past few weeks we have been tasked with the small-scale testing, full scale testing and overall reliability improvements of each event. As one of the few teams doing the whole RGM as one machine, we have run into a lot of problems requiring a lot of testing, innovation and problem solving to improve and finalise our designs. As a group we had to meticulously plan and organise the materials we needed, the times we were meeting and how to set up the machine. Initially when setting up the RGM we ran into a lot of problems. We began testing the first and second events and realised that our small-scale reliabilities did not translate well to the full-scale testing. The led to a lot of innovation and changing of designs within the first few events and the rest of the RGM. With continuous changes made to every event it was crucial that we set up the events right as we only had one shot to get it right. Unlike the other teams who could take days/weeks to perfect their events we ran into time constrains which meant our events were not as perfect as I would have liked however I am pleased with what we got done and happy that the construction is finished.
result: For the first 2 events we had to improve the reliability of the golf ball rolling down a table and knocking into a pendulum. Our reliability was basically non-existent with the ball rolling off the table, bouncing unpredictably and not going where we needed it. We had to test just the first event about 20 or so times before we got it right. To verify and validate the reliability of the event we had to make some major improvements with the limited resources we had. We found using tape as a sort of springy barrier worked well to dampen the bouncing of the golf ball. The innovative thinking that we as a group had to come up with was rather difficult yet rewarding when it worked. We also decided to split up the events to make sure they would work seamlessly whilst not taking us hours to get that one perfect event. We also realised that it was taking us a very long time to set up each event, with our first meeting together, we successfully created and filmed 7 events over 6 hours in week 10. We then planned for another meeting the following week, in which we finalised our RGM filming.
pfr: In order to test and verify a design within a team requires a lot of dedication. I never realised how hard the reliability stages of the design would be to overcome. Through hours of testing in person I thought that we had finally got it, but when we fixed one thing, another broke. During this process though, as a team we learnt how to deal with these challenges, often all of us working on it was too much. We split into smaller teams, whilst one was innovating and improving the design on one event, the others were preparing and testing the next event. This help workflow of the team and finishing off the events within the time we had allocated over the few days we had to construct the RGM. Testing takes time, a lot of time, and to finally verify and validate that an event has worked was rewarding. However in choosing to make the RGM as one whole machine was a challenge, yes we overcame it but was it worth it in the end? There are positives and negatives to taking this approach: (+) It made us work together better as a team, coming up with new ideas, building on others’ ideas and being able to set it up together as a whole. As a whole team, it felt very united and something we could all be proud of. When one person was struggling to improve the event they were working on, someone would come up with an idea. This was then implemented and improved upon and eventually validified by it working a majority of the time. As a group it was very enjoyable and social environment, this helped keep motivation high when testing failed and pushing for innovation within the designs (-) There were often times we got distracted. One group may have finished their event and were waiting on the others to finish on their design. At times we genuinely got bored and began mucking around which wasn’t the best for the productivity for our team. Other times people would take over leaving others with nothing to do but watch. Sometimes people would make suggestions, but they were ignored and put down, and often just getting something thrown together and finished was more important than actually improving the design.
learning: Honestly I’ve learnt that the final product in this case is not the most crucial thing to take away from this unit. I was so worried about everything being perfect, all the events looking perfect and working seamlessly. It was so much more important to focus on the innovation and creativity, with coming up with solutions to problems, which is at the heart of engineering itself. I thought having the most amazing filming angles and finished product would be all we were aiming for, but this isn’t the aspirations of the rest of the group. I found that not everyone will have the same end goal as me, but to work together and push each other was something that was inspiring. Throughout the last few weeks we have done extensive testing and reflecting on how we are improving and advancing in our designs, which has been an eye opening and rewarding experience. Again, much like what I reflected during the first 5 weeks, a lot of the seemingly easy steps throughout this designing, reliability and construction phase turned out to be quite difficult to navigate. It’s hard to swallow my pride and accept that not everyone is aiming for high marks with this unit, and that they just want to get this project done and over with. I hope that in some way I have convinced the others in my group to push themselves in the testing, validating and innovation of our machine, but in the end I’m happy with the friends that I’ve made during this unit and how much I’ve learnt throughout the engineering process and it relates to my future goals and career.

situation: During weeks one through eleven of ENGG1050, I was assigned to a group and instructed to work together to design, build, test, and record a functioning Rube Goldberg Machine (RGM). The recording had to combine each of our individual section action items to form one cohesive RGM that completed the task of putting an item in an open bin. In addition, we had weekly presentations where we would present our group's progress.
task_action: We began brainstorming ideas for a theme we could have for our RGM and originally decided on the theme of making a birthday cake. After we presented our idea to our tutor we received feedback that we should potentially downscale our project, which we did by changing our design to simply knocking a cake into a bin. We continued to make our weekly presentations and create our RGM over the holiday. We presented our documented testing results on reliability and our new iterations to our tutor group. Finally, we had our final designs of our RGM and are now about to soon submit our final video.
result: We were able to complete presentations ready to present weekly to our tutor group, and occasionally to the posse. We have our final design iteration of functioning RGM action items ready to record for the final video.
pfr: I have found that throughout this project, the online nature of the class has caused time and resource management to be slightly more difficult to determine. In the beginning, when deciding on a theme, we went too big in our idea and over-allocated time and resources that we, as university students, do not have. I personally as President of the Macquarie Machining Society am very busy, trying to balance school, running a society, and social life, in addition to trying to be conscious of my health by making sure to sleep enough and eat well. We as a group just underestimated how much a project of that scale would take timewise to execute, let alone the resources of space and materials to test the reliability of the cake-making RGM. Thankfully, under the advisement of our tutor, we were guided to scale back the size of our RGM to smaller sections, while still trying to keep to the overall theme of using a cake in a fun way. Another way the online nature of the course has been challenging in time management has been in creating the presentations. Being online has made it hard to contact people and arrange for them to do work both inside and outside of class. Oftentimes we will create a Google Slides presentation, however, will not fill in the content until late in the evening the night before we present. I myself have occasionally had to work late until the very early hours of the morning in order for the slideshow to be created, whereas a teammate may not have even opened the slideshow. While we have been successful enough so far to pass by, a way to improve this is by setting harsher deadlines and having a dedicated way to enforce those deadlines. Finally, the online nature of the course creates the challenge of group members turning off their cameras which makes it difficult to assign tasks as you do not know whether or not the member is at the computer. This has been a challenge for my group as two of my group members often do not have their cameras and microphones on during the online meeting. However, they do often attend in person meetings where they are more willing to help contribute to tasks assigned.
learning: By setting realistic goals and allocating resources efficiently, a project of this scale is very easy to accomplish and can be an enjoyable experience. However, when deadlines are not enforced it demotivates and does not hold people accountable, thereby creating stress and poor results, such as overtime presentations due to miscommunication over the content.

situation: This semester in ENGG3050, we were asked to research a startup and create a 4 minute presentation on a specific aspect of the company. This work was to be completed in groups of 5, and team members would need to collaborate in order to form cohesive presentations that flow on from each other. An extensive list of startups was provided to choose from, and group members could be chosen from students present in class. Specific research topics would be on a particular aspect of the startup's business operations and entrepreneurial journey, adhering to the Business Model Canvas components. The 5 research topics included: management structure and people/company culture, funding process and general business case, growth strategy and scaling journey, market opportunity and technical edge, and customer segment and product placement.
task_action: After forming groups, research would need to be undertaken to learn more about the startup and create a presentation relevant to the chosen company. We were encouraged to select a startup in an industry or market sector that interested us, to make researching the company more engaging and generate more enthusiasm during the presentation. After choosing a startup within the group, specific aspects of the startup would be selected by each member to conduct detailed research on. Prior to week 9, when the first member of our group would be presenting, my group planned to meet in-person and conduct research on the startup together, to allow for better collaboration and to encourage each other in our work. General research on the company would first be undertaken, to gain an understanding of who the startup is and what they do on the whole. In conducting this research, insight into the company's global expansion and inter-continental reach would be completed to develop an understanding of the importance of global perspectives and interactions. For some, companies, their geographic location or language may prevent them from expanding into new markets or making connections with overseas suppliers, manufacturers and customers. It is important to consider the global presence and the social, political and environmental landscape of a company, particularly when the company is from an area the researcher is unfamiliar with, considering standards and practices may be drastically different to that of Australia. ACTION: In my group, we selected to research and present on the EV charging and energy solutions startup Wallbox, which was founded in 2015 by two ex-tesla employees in Barcelona, Spain. After group deliberation, we decided that I would present on Topic D - Market Opportunity and Technological Edge. In researching Wallbox, I learned about how they progressed from presenting their prototype at startup pitch competitions to gain exposure and funds to making partnerships with international manufacturing chains to aid in their supply chains on a global scale. In the span of a decade, Wallbox progressed from a startup of two engineers, to a company with over 500 employees, 1 million customers worldwide and a valuation of $320 million. After gaining funding through winning a startup competition in 2016, angel investors in the late 2010s and 5 rounds of Series A VC funding in 2020, Wallbox was able to produce their first product for distribution within Spain. I found it interesting to learn about the large extent of the funding required to support the creation of an MVP and production, even though it was still limited to within the company's founding country at this stage. Wallbox initially had difficulty expanding their products into global markets, as company employees had little experience with overseas markets and foreign supply chains. Furthermore, the language barrier prevented CEO's Enric and Eduard from comfortably contacting potential business partners and investors. The somewhat turbulent political landscape in Spain combined with the lack of local manufacturers meant Wallbox had to look for alternative ways of designing and manufacturing their product. To overcome the language barrier and challenges imposed by the region the startup was founded in, Wallbox made the decision to hire employees overseas with better knowledge of the local area, to help assist them in global manufacturing and distribution. Knowing China's importance in global manufacturing given its ability to produce products on a large scale at low prices, Wallbox entered into a partnership with Changchun FAWSN, to become a key player in EV charger manufacturing in the region. The challenges faced by Wallbox in expanding into international markets reflects their inexperience and lack of knowledge of the global landscape.
result: In researching Wallbox and their experiences with global manufacturing and trade, I gained a greater insight into the global considerations and experiences that need to be taken into account when making business deals or considering international partnerships. While it's easy to assume that all humans, or in this instance CEOs and business owners, have similar views and experiences to that of yourself, however this simply isn't true. Each individual is uniquely shaped by the environment they live in and their life experiences. How people choose to respond to these often negative life experiences is what shapes them as a person. Similarly, companies are moulded by the industry they operate in, their country of origin and the business decisions made by those in charge of the company. Particularly when considering countries other than Australia, the living conditions, political stability, civil status and environmental landscape can influence company experiences and culture. In researching Spanish startup Wallbox, I have learned about the factors that come into play when making decisions on a global scale and how differences in opinion and experience can be resultant of unique environments within a particular country. This experience has helped me develop a global perspective and understanding of the unique circumstances that shape individuals and businesses on an international scale.
pfr: In researching my chosen company Wallbox, I felt intrigued by the business decisions made and the circumstances that informed their decision making at the time. After struggling to secure funding, Wallbox branched out of their comfort zone to secure partnerships with a Chinese manufacturing company, despite the geographical and language barriers. The CEOs of Wallbox themselves expressed their hesitation with the business move, as they had no idea what to expect. However, Wallbox chose to embrace the partnership, and within a year, the two companies had become synonymous, with Wallbox expressing their profound gratitude for the Chinese company. The positive experience Wallbox had encouraged them to expand further into Asian EV markets and even start new partnerships with countries in other continents, including North America, Africa, Oceana and Europe. In 2018, Wallbox underwent a culture shift when looking to expand beyond the Spanish market and venture in to new areas. Instead of relying on hard data and quantitative information, Wallbox took into consideration the qualitative aspects of potential partnerships with new regions, and saw the benefit of incorporating the unique ideas and perspectives of individuals from other countries into their workforce and target market. This shift from relying on knowledge-based concepts for business direction to considering mindset-based improvements and perspectives allowed the company to expand into new territories with great success. Researching and understanding Wallbox's progression from a small Spanish startup working out of a one room warehouse to a global powerhouse in EV charging production with customers in 80 countries has been intriguing, informative and impactful. Their experience has allowed me to see the merit in considering how a situation or problem impacts not just myself, but also how the scenario relates to people around the world.
learning: Researching and learning about the experience of Wallbox has taught me the importance of considering the impact of ones surroundings and environment on who they are, whether it be a person, or a large company. On a global scale, the majority of people have different life experiences to myself and have been moulded by a combination of factors including the political landscape, unique experiences, the environment and leadership schemes. It's crucial to never judge a person (or company for that matter) on face value and instead take the time to understand why something is the way that it is. I have also learned the importance of respecting the opinions and views of diverse countries, cultures, heritages, ages and lifestyles. Collaborating with individuals and entities substantially different to yourself can be extremely beneficial as they bring unique perspectives and opinions to a situation that can help improve a design or situation. For example, Wallbox had limited knowledge of the Asian EV market, however collaboration with Chinese manufacturing company Changchun FAWSN helped them gain insights into the Chinese EV landscape to better understand what consumers would be expecting of them. This helped Wallbox to develop a viable product for the EV market that met the unique charging, time and location parameters of global customers. Wallbox's experiences have helped me to develop a global perspective, and consider the impact situations may have on others, depending on their personal experiences and the environment in which they operate. Adjusting the lens through which I see the world around me will help me better empathise with people and understand where they are coming from when their opinions, ideas and experiences may differ to my own. I have learned to consider the complex nature of people and companies, whilst considering the different viewpoints that guide their decision making, the cultural perspectives that shape their experiences and the global extent to which issues may impact others around the world.

situation: During my Second year at university, I participated in a group project for our engineering course. Our assignment was to design a 200mm cube that allowed marbles to travel through a series of interconnected events. This disagreement risked delaying the project and creating lasting tension between the teams, potentially jeopardizing our collaborative efforts and project success.
task_action: My responsibility was to mediate between the two teams to find a compromise that would enable us to stay on schedule and meet the expectations of both the Motions and Structures teams. I needed to facilitate a solution that would keep the project moving forward without sacrificing the integrity of the final product. ACTION: To address the conflict, I took the following steps: * INITIAL MEETINGS: I arranged individual meetings with both teams to thoroughly understand their perspectives and concerns. During this discussion, I stressed the importance of teamwork and mutual respect. * BRAINSTORMING SOLUTIONS: Together, we brainstormed potential compromises. One suggestion was to incorporate a rolling staircase mechanism powered by a DC motor, allowing the marbles to exit through the top of the cube. * DEVELOPING A REVISED PLAN: Based on our brainstorming session, we created a revised project plan that included a clear timeline for the initial launch and subsequent updates, along with checkpoints to monitor progress and quality. * ONGOING COMMUNICATION: I set up regular follow-up meetings to track the project's progress and ensure both teams remained aligned, promptly addressing any new issues that arose.
result: The conflict was successfully resolved, and we launched a prototype that satisfied both teams. The initial cube launch was completed on schedule, enabling the Motions team to take advantage of the delivery and presentation. Subsequent updates were released as planned, maintaining the quality standards of the product. This outcome not only achieved the project’s objectives but also enhanced the working relationship between the teams. pfr: I was first both nervous and responsible as I knew that my ability to mediate will determine how well the project turned out. That being said, as the conversations went on and the two teams started speaking more honestly, I became more assured and satisfied with their desire to cooperate. learning: From this experience, I learned several critical lessons: * EMPATHY AND UNDERSTANDING: It was essential to spend time understanding and listening to the issues of each workgroup. I became aware of the significance of leading discussions in a way that promotes respectful discourse and constructive disagreement. * FLEXIBILITY AND CREATIVITY: It frequently takes creativity and adaptability to find a workable solution. A direct outcome of this method was the phased launch solution, which shows how creative ideas may come from group discussion. FUTURE ACTIONS: In disagreements down the road, I'll: * Make empathy and attentive listening your top priorities to make sure you comprehend all relevant viewpoints. * Guide talks and make sure all opinions are heard by using structured facilitation approaches. * Aim for innovative ideas that take into account the needs of all stakeholders by encouraging brainstorming sessions. * In order to stop disputes from getting worse, establish clear communication procedures and frequent check-ins right away. Through contemplation, I have gained a deeper comprehension of the significance of compromise, negotiation, and dispute resolution in project management. My dedication to creating a cooperative and courteous work atmosphere has been strengthened by the acquisition of useful tactics to tackle analogous circumstances in the future.

situation: I was developing a new engineering solution to address the parking problem at Macquarie University in the 5-7 workshop weeks. Given the innovative nature of my approach, which aimed to create a system that could efficiently determine the availability of parking spots and alert users when they were full, I was keen on protecting my intellectual property (IP) to secure a competitive edge in the market. However, considering my limited resources and expertise in IP law, I faced challenges in determining the most effective pathway to protect and commercialise my technology.
task_action: My task was to identify and implement a suitable IP protection strategy and patent law that would not only safeguard my invention but also facilitate its successful commercialisation. I needed to evaluate various options, such as licensing, joint ventures, spin-offs, acquisitions, and in-house development, and select the most feasible approach for my situation. To address this, I formed a dedicated working group comprising engineers, legal advisors, and business development experts. I began by conducting a thorough analysis of my technology to determine which aspects could be protected by patents, trademarks, copyrights, or trade secrets. I then evaluated the commercial pathways available to me: 1. Licensing: I considered licensing my technology to established companies with the resources to bring it to market quickly. 2. Joint Ventures: I explored potential partnerships with other firms to share the development risks and costs. 3. Spin-offs: I discussed the possibility of creating a subsidiary focused solely on the new technology. 4. Acquisition: I looked into acquiring or merging with a company that had complementary technology and market presence. 5. In-house Development: I assessed my capability to develop and commercialise the technology independently. Using the gallery method of brainstorming, I generated and assessed these options, considering factors such as resource availability, expertise, time-to-market, and potential return on investment. Each option was evaluated based on predefined parameters, including cost, complexity, and strategic fit with my long-term goals.
result: After a detailed evaluation, I decided to pursue a combination of licensing and in-house development. Licensing the core technology allowed me to generate immediate revenue and leverage the commercialization capabilities of my partners. Simultaneously, I retained in-house development of specific components to maintain control over key innovations and ensure continued improvement of my technology. As a result: * I secured multiple licensing agreements with leading companies in my industry, generating a steady stream of revenue. * I successfully patented several critical aspects of my technology, providing strong IP protection and enhancing my market position. * My in-house development team continued to innovate, leading to the creation of additional patentable features and improvements. * The dual approach enabled me to enter the market faster while maintaining strategic control over my most valuable IP assets. Overall, the chosen IP protection strategy and patent law not only safeguarded my invention but also facilitated its successful commercialization, contributing to the company's growth and market competitiveness.
pfr: At the outset, the task of protecting and commercialising my innovative technology for solving the parking problem at Macquarie University felt quite overwhelming. Intellectual property and patent law were areas where I had limited expertise, and the stakes were high for my company's future. The complexity of the various pathways for IP protection and commercialization added to the challenge, and I initially felt uncertain about the best approach to take. However, as I formed a working group and systematically evaluated my options, my confidence grew. Collaborating with engineers, legal advisors, and business development experts provided a wealth of perspectives that enriched our discussions. Documenting each step of my decision-making process and using a structured method to assess the merits of each option helped me navigate the complexity and come to a consensus. Through this experience, I realized the power of interdisciplinary collaboration and systematic analysis. The process not only demystified the intricacies of IP protection but also fostered a strong sense of teamwork and shared purpose. By breaking down the problem into manageable parts and rigorously evaluating each option, I was able to make informed decisions that aligned with my strategic goals.
learning: This experience taught me several valuable lessons about intellectual property, strategic decision-making, and the importance of collaborative problem-solving. One key insight was the realization that there is no one-size-fits-all solution when it comes to IP protection and commercialisation. Each option—whether licensing, joint ventures, spin-offs, acquisitions, or in-house development—has its own set of advantages and trade-offs. The best choice depends on a company’s specific circumstances, resources, and long-term objectives. I also learned the importance of a merit-based approach in decision-making. By establishing clear criteria and evaluating each option against these parameters, I was able to objectively assess the best path forward. This structured approach not only facilitated more effective decision-making but also ensured that all team members were aligned and committed to the chosen strategy. In the future, I will approach similar challenges with a greater appreciation for the importance of interdisciplinary collaboration and systematic analysis. I will prioritize bringing together diverse expertise to tackle complex problems and will ensure that decision-making processes are transparent and well-documented. Additionally, I will remain open to exploring multiple pathways and will rigorously evaluate each option to find the most strategic and viable solution. * Overall, this experience has deepened my understanding of intellectual property and its critical role in protecting and commercializing innovative technologies. It has also reinforced the value of a structured, collaborative approach to decision-making, which I will carry forward in my professional endeavours.
