topic: Initiative and the willingness to make decisions in the face of uncertainty
situation: In my third-year unit, CIVL3301 (Design of Concrete Structures), my group was tasked with designing a carpark structure on campus. This project required us to plan and virtually design a structurally sound carpark that adhered to relevant Australian Standards (AS). We faced significant challenges in identifying the appropriate standards to follow. There were also uncertainties regarding the minimum/appropriate measurements for car spaces, parking spaces, turning radii, and the design of pedestrian access points such as lift shafts, stairs, and ramps.
task_action: Our group had to overcome these uncertainties by identifying the correct Australian Standards and making informed assumptions about the various measurements needed for our design. We aimed to develop a comprehensive and compliant design report for the parking lot structure that addressed all specifications and constraints. ACTION: To tackle these challenges, we took the initiative to organise a series of focused meetings within the group. In these meetings, we divided the project into smaller, manageable sections, assigning specific tasks to each group member based on their strengths and areas of expertise. For the Australian Standards, I reached out to our convenor for guidance and also consulted online databases (i.e. SAI Global and MQ Multisearch) to gather the necessary information and AS documentation. With the assumptions regarding measurements, we conducted a comparative study of existing parking lot structures on and off campus (i.e. comparing the South 2 Carpark with Bella Vista Metro Station's carpark), collecting data on average dimensions and layouts (tape measuring and counting spaces) and taking photos for future reference. This research allowed us to make educated assumptions for our design.
result: Our proactive and multipronged approach and willingness to navigate through uncertainty resulted in the design report being completed. We identified all the relevant Australian Standards for our project and made cautious assumptions about the design measurements. The final design was compliant with the necessary standards.
pfr: At the beginning, facing the project felt like we were thrown into a marathon we weren't ready for at all - taking many steps to reach the finishline. The task of adhering to Australian Standards while dealing with uncertain measurements seemed tough to figure out from afar. It was daunting, knowing that our decisions had to be correctly accurate despite not having all the information we needed. However, as we progressed through working on aspects of the project, things became clearer when we tackled these challenges head-on. It was rewarding to see our project take shape, transforming my initial unsurity into confidence in what we were completing as a group.
learning: Despite our uncertainty, this experience reinforced the importance of taking initiative and the willingness to make informed decisions. I see the power of teamwork and how each team member's perspective and skillset allowed the project to be successfully completed as planned. Breaking down complex multi-faceted issues into manageable chunks to systematically resolve them triumphs as the best strategy for such cases like this group project. This approach showed me that a productive and collaborative workspace is fostered when coupled with effective decision-making (even as decentralised group members, compared to a typical top-down hierarchical leader). I have come to understand that uncertainty is a natural feeling that comes with undertaking a project on any level and that the key to it is approaching it with confidence and assurance that putting my mind to it will help me find solutions.

situation: In my ENGG4001 Professional Practice course, my team were confronted with the theoretical challenge of designing a water purification plant. A significant pain point in such infrastructure is the reliance on non-renewable energy sources, which conflicts with modern sustainability goals.
task_action: With my major in Electronics and Electrical Engineering, I was tasked with investigating potential energy sources for the plant. situation: During the project of my engineering course, my team faced a significant challenge. We were tasked with designing a cost-effective water purification system for rural communities. The initial concept was promising, but initial tests revealed it was less effective in removing contaminants than required by safety standards.
task_action: As the project leader, my primary task was to enhance our design to meet safety standards without escalating costs prohibitively. It was crucial to maintain the project's viability by keeping the solution both effective and economically feasible. Action: I initiated a series of critical thinking sessions with the team. We began by analyzing the existing design to pinpoint inefficiencies and potential areas for improvement. Using a structured problem-solving approach, we listed all possible modifications, such as integrating a more efficient filtration material or redesigning the flow system to increase contact time with the filter. Each idea was critically evaluated based on its potential impact on contaminant removal and cost implications. We also consulted with our professors and industry experts to gain insights and validate our findings.
result: Through these critical thinking exercises, we selected and implemented a dual-stage filtration system that significantly increased the purification efficacy without a substantial cost increase. The redesigned system not only met the safety standards but also remained within the budget constraints. This approach not only resolved the initial problem but also enhanced our team's ability to tackle complex issues systematically. The project received commendable feedback for its innovation and practical applicability. This experience underscored the value of critical thinking in engineering, enabling us to deliver a solution that was both technically sound and economically viable.
pfr: The initial encounter with the challenge of enhancing our water purification system was quite intimidating. As project leader, the responsibility felt immense, not just in terms of meeting the technical specifications, but also in guiding my team effectively through the uncertainty. Initially, I was anxious about the possibility of not finding a feasible solution within the constraints. However, as we progressed through the critical thinking sessions, I felt a growing confidence. It was empowering to see the team's collective intellect converging on practical solutions. The process of dissecting the problem, analyzing each component, and consulting with experts brought a sense of clarity and purpose that gradually replaced my initial apprehension with optimism.
learning: This experience has profoundly impacted how I view problem-solving in engineering. One of the key insights I gained is the importance of structured critical thinking and open communication in driving successful outcomes. By methodically breaking down the problem and evaluating each potential solution based on predefined criteria, we were able to make informed decisions that aligned with our project goals. This approach not only streamlined the decision-making process but also ensured that all team members were on the same page, which enhanced collaboration and reduced the potential for conflict. In future projects, I intend to apply this structured critical thinking approach more consistently from the outset. I've learned that early and thorough analysis, combined with ongoing evaluation and adaptation, is crucial in managing complex engineering challenges. Additionally, fostering an environment where team members feel encouraged to voice their ideas and concerns will be a priority. This project taught me that effective leadership in engineering is as much about facilitating the right conversations as it is about making the final decisions.

situation: IN MY SECOND YEAR OF ENGINEERING, OUR TEAM WAS TASKED WITH DESIGNING AN AUTOMATIC TEA MAKER. task_action: As a team member, my role was to contribute to the analysis and redesign of our control system to ensure that our automatic tea maker would theoretically produce high-quality tea consistently. Action: We organized several group troubleshooting sessions where we critically analyzed our initial control system design. Using critical thinking techniques, we identified potential issues such as sensor inaccuracies and timing mismatches. We also sought feedback from our professors and peers to refine our design. This iterative process included brainstorming sessions to generate new ideas and using decision matrices to evaluate the feasibility and impact of each proposed solution.
result: Through our collaborative critical thinking approach, we were able to identify and address the theoretical inconsistencies in our control system. We made several design changes, such as improving sensor accuracy and refining the timing algorithms. After thorough theoretical testing and validation, our design for the automatic tea maker consistently met the desired specifications. The project was completed successfully and received positive feedback for its innovative approach and thoroughness. This experience highlighted the importance of critical thinking and teamwork in solving complex engineering problems.
pfr: Initially, I felt frustrated and anxious about the inconsistencies in our automatic tea maker design. The pressure to deliver a functional and reliable design was daunting. However, as we engaged in critical thinking and collaborative problem-solving, my confidence grew. Encouraging open discussion and questioning of our assumptions fostered a more collaborative and productive team environment. By the end of the project, I felt a deep sense of satisfaction and accomplishment in our ability to overcome the challenges through systematic analysis and teamwork.
learning: This experience taught me the value of critical thinking and collaboration in engineering projects. situation: To complete quiz 2 on "The House of Quality" by John R. Hauser and Don Clausing, I came across a real-world situation that called for employing the concepts covered in the class. In particular, the quiz asked participants to compare Toyota's improved rust prevention techniques with the design choices made by an American fast car maker on where to put the emergency brake lever.
task_action: I read the information in the magazine from May 1988 in great detail before taking the quiz. It was essential to comprehend the House of Quality idea and how it applied to quality function deployment (QFD). I answered the quiz by dissecting the prerequisites since I knew the material well. Firstly, I examined the provided scenario, which contrasted Toyota's improved rust prevention strategy with the location of the emergency brake lever on an American sports vehicle. Secondly, I determined the engineering characteristics (ECs) and customer attributes (CAs) pertinent to each scenario by using the House of Quality's tenets. In the case of the emergency brake lever, CAs may include driver accessibility, whereas ECs might include safety and ergonomic design. thirdly, I created a connection matrix map that showed how every technical choice affected how customers saw it. This required assessing each EC's importance in reaching the targeted CAs. Finally, Based on the data, I came to certain conclusions and made some main ideas in my mind, This will help me in answering quiz 2.
result: After this article, My ability to demonstrate a thorough comprehension of the principles and their practical ramifications was demonstrated by applying the House of Quality framework to the exam scenario. The end product was a thorough study and a solution proposal that skillfully combined engineering concerns with customer objectives. This strategy not only demonstrated my mastery of the subject matter but also offered insightful information on the significance of quality control and customer-centric design in product development. and I receive a decent grade for it as well.
pfr: When I had to go through "The House of Quality" in Quiz 2, at first, I was a little overwhelmed. I wasn't sure whether I could properly analyze and apply the principles to events in the actual world since they looked complicated. I was able to answer the quiz questions and come to reasonable conclusions by methodically using the House of Quality framework. I also discovered how important it is to weigh engineering features and consumer demands while making design decisions. situation: During the third workshop in my COMP2250 course, we were given a dataset on statistical patterns and alloted to conduct speculation testing. This circumstance was basic in understanding how to utilise measurable strategies to approve our discoveries and guard them against examination. The workshop was expecting to recreate real-world information examination scenarios in which data-driven choices are basic.
task_action: The task was to develop a hypothesis about the dataset and test it with appropriate statistical methods. I specifically hypothesised that there is a significant difference in average income between two demographic groups in the dataset. The goal was to use hypothesis testing techniques to confirm or reject this hypothesis, ensuring that our analysis was rigorous and statistically sound. To begin this task, I conducted an exploratory data analysis (EDA) to become acquainted with the dataset and identify key variables and potential outliers. I then developed both the null hypothesis (no significant difference in average income) and the alternative hypothesis (significant difference in average income). Using Python, I used statistical libraries like pandas for data manipulation and sciPy to perform a t-test to compare the two groups' means. Throughout the process, I meticulously documented my steps and ensured that my code was repeatable and simple to understand. I also consulted with peers and instructors to confirm my approach and interpretations.
result: The analysis revealed a statistically significant difference in average incomes between the two demographic groups, resulting in the rejection of the null hypothesis. This result confirmed my hypothesis and provided useful information about potential socioeconomic disparities. The successful application of hypothesis testing not only validated our methodological approach, but also demonstrated the value of statistical analysis in drawing meaningful conclusions from data. The results were well received during the workshop presentation, demonstrating the practical value of rigorous data analysis and hypothesis testing in real-world scenarios.
pfr: Initially, the task of hypothesis testing in the COMP2250 workshop seemed intimidating. The prospect of rigorously analysing a dataset and defending the results appeared overwhelming, especially given the high stakes associated with statistical significance. However, as I approached the problem systematically, performing exploratory data analysis (EDA) and documenting each step, I gained confidence. The STAR framework's clear structure enabled me to divide the task into manageable parts, making the process less daunting. Collaborating with peers and getting feedback from instructors also helped to alleviate my initial concerns. By the end of the workshop, I felt a sense of accomplishment and empowerment because I knew I had used statistical methods correctly and reached meaningful conclusions.
learning: This experience taught me the value of a methodical, structured approach to data analysis. The STAR framework helped me stay organised and focused, and the hypothesis testing process demonstrated the importance of evidence-based conclusions. I also realised the importance of thorough documentation and reproducibility in data analysis, as they help not only understand but also defend results. Moving forward, I will continue to use these structured methodologies to ensure that my analyses are sound and defendable. In addition, I learned how important collaboration and feedback are in the learning process. Consulting with peers and instructors provided a variety of perspectives and helped me refine my approach. This experience taught me to seek and value feedback as an important part of my learning process. In the future, I will act differently by: 1.Emphasising the importance of thorough documentation and reproducibility in my work. 2.Continue to seek feedback from peers and instructors to improve my analyses. 3.Utilising structured methodologies, such as the STAR framework, to divide complex tasks into manageable chunks. 4.Being more confident in my ability to tackle difficult analytical tasks using systematic approaches and collaboration. Overall, this experience has greatly increased my confidence and competence in hypothesis testing and data analysis, giving me valuable skills for my future academic and professional endeavours.

situation: Our goal was to brainstorm functional designs for our heating and cooling components in the Internet Tea Maker creatively.

I enjoyed the creative freedom it allowed us; we could create a design, flesh out someone else's design or combine ideas together, if we saw fit. 2) Decision Matrix The decision matrix was vital as a creative tool in filtering through our creative ideas. topic: The design process phasing and approaches
situation: In our engineering design course, we were charged with creating a new tea maker that could not only brew tea but also add honey and butter to the cup once it was ready. The objective was to create a dependable mechanism that could correctly distribute honey and butter into the cup without interfering with the overall performance of the tea maker.
task_action: The purpose of the brainstorming session was to come up with a practical design for this dispensing mechanism. The primary considerations were the differences in viscosity and melting points between honey and butter, as well as ensuring that the mechanism was simple to clean and maintain. Our goal was to create a design for this device that blended perfectly with our main tea maker design while meeting all safety and usability regulations. We employed the gallery style of brainstorming, in which each team member separately generated multiple design ideas. We then placed all of the suggestions on a whiteboard for everyone to see. We assessed each offered solution using particular criteria such as weight, complexity, manufacturability, ease of cleaning, and cost. We ranked the proposals according to their feasibility and efficacy. This helped us reduce the list down to six potential options.
result: I successfully chose a design solution for my design from among the six choices generated during the brainstorming session. The preferred design included a dual-chamber system with a heating element for butter and a precision pump for honey.
pfr: In our engineering design course, we were charged with creating a new tea maker that could not only brew tea but also add honey and butter to the cup once it was ready. As the designer, I was responsible for making all design decisions and I felt overwhelmed because I was designing a unique sort of tea maker I had not thought of before. However, after I organized a brainstorming session with my mates to gather ideas it started to become less of a burden. I was surprised by how there were so many other possibilities out there that I had not thought of. situation: During the semester, as a group we were required to produce a design for a tea machine, whereby we were given a series of specific customer wants and needs, of which we had to incorporate into our machine. Some of these conditions could be conflicting, so we had to ensure that we chose the extent to which each condition would be included and how it would effect the machine.
task_action: Each individual member of the group designed their own machine and incorporated the components in their own way. After the completion of each members machine design, we then got together and discussed the pros and cons of each machine, and any notable ideas that should be incorporated into the final product. This communication process was important as it would ensure that the final product would have as many of the best ideas that we each came up with, and as few of the bad ideas. We also noticed that many of our ideas were the same, which reinforced our reasoning as to why that specific idea/component should be included.
result: The result of this communication collaboration was that we were able to produce and incorporate the best ideas that we could think of across the group, meaning that our final product would be at a greater quality than if we had never contributed our own ideas to the group. Since the tea machine assignment is an individual assignment, we now all have a greater expansion of ideas that we have gained from each other, compared to if we had only used our own individual designs.
pfr: Initially, there was some confusion as to how the tea machine should look or function, and to what extent each of the customers needs and wants should be included. We found that as we began to share ideas with each other, we gradually became much more clear on how the final product should look, and we gained a greater insight as to how we wanted the product to actually work and function. We were able to use each others ideas to determine what we liked and didn't like about our own initial designs, which allowed us to tweak and modify our own products to greater fit the needs that had been given to us.
learning: By using a communication and collaborative based approach to the problem at hand, we were able to make the best possible decisions regarding how the machine should look and function, as well as how we should incorporate the customers needs and wants. We realised that the approach we used could be applied to almost any problem, given each member had the correct experience in the field. It helped us understand that in order to produce the best product possible, given your constraints, a collaborative approach is often the best approach to take as it will allow for the most ideas to be shared and contemplated.

situation: Defining requirements for a tea maker connected to the internet from a small list of customer wants and from interacting with the customer.
task_action: In newly formed groups, we analysed the original list of customer requirements and split them into requirements that could be fulfilled and requirements on which we needed more clarification from the customer. We then went through the customer correspondence with other groups, updated our requirements based on the answers, and asked additional questions. Once we felt we had a baseline understanding of the customer requirements (little confusion) we began brainstorming ideas based on these requirements.
result: The result was a well-defined list of requirements that reflected the customer's wants including TPM's which was used for future brainstorming and design stages.
pfr: While we all had experience with the conceptual design phase (product defining, brainstorming etc.) this activity was more technical than we were used to and so at the start, there was a lot of confusion as to technical concepts (TPM's) and how to approach a customer actively giving responses to questions and changing requirements. We also felt frustration with the customer as he was not always clear on what he wanted, made conflicting requests for the machine and was not technically illiterate in the ways of networking (Internet) and either made impossible requests (no data saved but the requirement of sharing tea recipes with friends over the internet) or general confusing requests (butter compartment in tea maker to put butter in tea). We were frustrated but determined to accommodate as best we could for all requests and in the end, we picked our battles and ended with a list of requirements and the beginnings of a list of TPMs and brainstorming the design.
learning: While I knew that in my career I would encounter projects in which the requests seem confusing or unrealistic and customers who are confused, technically illiterate and have conflicting ideas, I had never had experience with this. All of us as a group learned to pick and choose our battles in terms of interacting with the customer and coming up with requirements, we also learned to compromise with these requirements. For example, with the requirement of no data saving, we came up with a solution in which all data shared with friends (recipe) will be deleted after a week. Within that week, friends can rate and review the recipe and save it to their machine if they want to use it. That way all data is temporarily in a database and not saved permanently, all data saved will not be user-specific (only tea recipes). We made many compromises we felt best fulfilled the customer's wants without being unachievable. Through this experience, I now have a greater understanding and expectations for projects in future and have practice in making these compromises when conversing with the customer.

situation: My team at the software startup where I interned was tasked with creating a new feature for our product that would increase user engagement. However, user feedback revealed that the feature was falling short of expectations due to its excessive complexity and lack of user-friendliness following the initial development period.
task_action: I was given the responsibility of managing a small team to reevaluate and rethink the functionality as a junior developer. Simplifying the functionality without sacrificing its ability to achieve the initial goal of raising user engagement was a challenge. ACTION: To fully comprehend the criticism, I started a series of critical thinking meetings with all the stakeholders. We used a variety of critical thinking techniques, including brainstorming sessions to come up with solutions and root cause analysis to determine why the feature was not user-friendly. Every meeting sought to disprove our presumptions and objectively consider every option. We painstakingly recorded every meeting, emphasise important ideas and workable solutions.
result: These sessions of critical thinking produced a redesigned functionality that was more user-friendly and in line with user expectations. We saw a 40% boost in user engagement after relaunching the feature, and the response we received thereafter was very favourable. This experience strengthened my capacity to use critical thinking successfully in software development, in addition to improving the final product. This reflection shows how using critical thinking to address problems in the real world in an organised and efficient way can result in quantifiable gains and individual growth in problem-solving abilities.
pfr: Leading a feature redesign as a junior developer was frightening at first. I was worried about my capacity to refute the status quo and offer workable alternatives. I was surprisingly surprised by how insightful the structured critical thinking sessions were, despite my reservations. I became aware of the effectiveness of cooperative problem-solving after speaking with many stakeholders face-to-face and hearing their opinions. Seeing how several viewpoints may result in a straightforward solution that suited user demands was motivating.
learning: This event has greatly influenced how I see software development problem-solving techniques. I discovered that critical thinking involves more than just identifying errors; it also entails comprehending the underlying causes of those errors and cooperating to find a solution. My main learnings were the value of empathy in comprehending consumer feedback and the efficiency of organised brainstorming sessions. I'll give these strategies more weight in problem-solving situations going forward to make sure that user input and group discussions are central to the development process. Furthermore, even as a junior team member, this experience has motivated me to advocate and propose solutions with more assertiveness. I now have a greater respect for critical thinking's systematic, logical approach to problem-solving as a result of this experience. I'll be using these guidelines more widely from here on, not just when responding to user input but also when anticipating problems early on in the design process. This is probably going to result in more robust and user-focused product features.

situation: Throughout the semester, we had to design an IoT tea machine that could cater to user preferences via a smartphone app. The designing of this project required close collaboration of our multidisciplinary team, which included three civil engineers and three software engineers, working hand in hand.
task_action: We had to ensure that all components of the IoT tea machine worked harmoniously together. The civil engineers were responsible for the physical design of the machine, while the software engineers developed the app design and integrated the machine’s functionalities. We worked towards our shared objective by distributing every role and responsibilities according to our discipline, setting up regular meetings, clarifying requirements, and addressing any emerging issues promptly. Importantly, we didn't work in isolation; the software and the civil engineers cross-checked and supported each other's work to ensure that the system was feasible as a whole. For instance, when the civil engineers encountered a challenge with the machine’s water heating mechanism, the software engineers also brainstormed together and explored a potential solution: a dispenser that could heat up the required amount of water on demand without compromising the machine's structural integrity. Therefore, by leveraging our collective expertise, we devised a solution that integrated the heat-up-on the-go dispensers seamlessly into the design.
result: As a result, we achieved our targets by designing an efficient tea machine that fits exactly to the customer's requirements; allowing users to customise the tea preferences via the app and share the tea recipe within a friend's group. This successful outcome was a testament to the power of effective teamwork and the combined efforts of engineers from varying disciplines.
pfr: Based on my experience of working on the IoT tea machine project, I realise that the teamwork of multidisciplinary engineers played the most significant role in our success. Our team consisted of three civil engineers and three software engineers, which helped us to integrate the physical design and software functionality effectively. My feelings while working on this design had a fusion of excitement and some moments of stress, particularly when balancing the different working procedures and priorities of the team members. The civil engineers were primarily focused on the building materials, structure, functionality, aligning the components and overall aesthetics, while the software engineers focused on developing a user-friendly app and establishing connectivity. These differences sometimes led to misunderstandings and delays. For instance, it took us a good amount of time to explain the app’s features to the civil teammates, so that they can keep track while proceeding each step of the design. There were disagreements at some points as well, when I felt a bit overwhelmed, but later it helped me to realise the importance of respecting others opinions and analysing and working on them constructively. To navigate such challenges, I actively facilitated communication, organised regular meetings, and ensured that everyone understood the project's overall goals and their specific responsibilities, and got the chance for making and mentality for accepting constructive criticism.
learning: From this project, I learned that productivity underlies effective teamwork and shared responsibilities. Clear communication, and conflict resolution techniques were the key to overcoming the challenges we faced. This experience has significantly influenced my life as a future engineer, highlighting the importance of empathy, active listening, and mediation skills. Moving forward, I plan to enhance my expertise by practicing all the soft skills that I have learned here. By applying these strategies, I aim to foster a collaborative environment in my professional life, ensuring that all team members feel valued and understood, and their roles are distributed as per their specialisations and preferences. It will help me act more confidently, contributing to the success of complex future engineering projects.

situation: In my engineering design course, my team was tasked with designing an innovative tea maker. The goal was to design a tea-making automation tool that would be simple to use and produce excellent tea. We had a lot of ideas from our first brainstorming meetings, but we had trouble coming up with a concept that was simple, functional, and feasible to produce.
task_action: Recognizing the need for structured creative thinking, We formed a small working group and clearly articulated the problem statement: design a tea maker that automates brewing, offers customizable options for different types of tea, and is easy to clean and use. Each team member was given the task of sketching their ideas on paper and displaying them around the room. During this process, I facilitated the discussion to ensure everyone’s ideas were heard and evaluated fairly. We used criteria such as user-friendliness, ease of cleaning, brewing customization options, and potential manufacturing challenges to assess each concept. This structured approach allowed us to combine the best features from different designs into a cohesive solution.
result: By the end, we had generated six viable design options. We ranked these based on the established criteria and selected a final design that incorporated the most beneficial aspects of each idea. This final design featured an intuitive interface for customizing brewing parameters, a detachable infuser for easy cleaning, and a compact form factor suitable for various kitchen sizes.
pfr: At the outset, the task of designing a tea maker felt quite overwhelming. The complexity of automating a simple yet nuanced process such as tea making, while ensuring ease of use and manufacturability, seemed daunting. Initially, our brainstorming sessions were chaotic, with no clear direction. I felt a mix of excitement and frustration – excitement about the potential innovation and frustration about our lack of progress. When I proposed a more systematic approach to our brainstorming, I felt somewhat anxious about how the team would respond. However, as we began organizing our ideas and discussing them in detail, I felt a sense of relief and satisfaction. This structured approach allowed us to channel our creativity productively, and seeing our ideas take shape helped clarify our thinking. I felt proud of my role in facilitating the discussion and ensuring that everyone’s ideas were considered. By the end of our sessions, I felt a significant sense of accomplishment. We moved from a state of confusion to a clear, agreed-upon design direction. This transformation reinforced my belief in the power of structured creative processes and effective teamwork.
learning: From this experience, I learned several valuable lessons about creative thinking and team dynamics. In future projects, I will continue to apply structured creative techniques, ensuring that our brainstorming sessions are both productive and inclusive. I will also place greater emphasis on clear criteria for decision-making and remain open to adapting and combining ideas to arrive at the best possible solutions. This experience has given me a deeper appreciation for the interplay between creativity, structure, and collaboration in engineering design.

situation: While working on one of my software design units, our team was tasked with designing a complex game using Processing and managing the project on GitHub where we had faced some major conflicts. These disputes led to fragmented code contributions, inconsistent design elements, and a stalled project timeline.
task_action: I had become the team mediator with my primary task being resolving conflicts, negotiating and conciliating everyone's views to a single point, and ensuring a cohesive and efficient development progress. It was crucial to balance different creative perspectives while keeping the project on track and maintaining a collaborative atmosphere. Action : To address the conflicts within the team, I facilitated open communication by organizing a meeting where everyone could voice their opinions and concerns. We redefined the game's core objectives and documented them in a shared project roadmap on GitHub. I introduced a voting system for major design decisions to ensure a democratic process and set up coding standards to maintain code quality and consistency. We utilized GitHub Issues and Projects boards to enhance task management and established a conflict resolution protocol with regular check-ins and a designated mediator.
result: These actions led to a unified vision for the game, with improved coherence in mechanics and design. The implementation of coding standards and regular reviews streamlined development, resulting in higher quality code. Enhanced collaboration through GitHub tools increased productivity and accountability. The team successfully completed the game within the revised timeline, with improved morale and cohesion due to transparent conflict resolution and democratic decision-making processes.
pfr: Initially, I felt a mixture of frustration and determination. The discord within the team was disheartening, especially given the project's potential and our initial enthusiasm. However, I also felt a strong sense of responsibility and a drive to resolve the issues. The core issues stemmed from a lack of clear communication and unified vision at the outset. The team’s diverse perspectives, while valuable, led to disagreements that hindered progress. However, with our collaborative efforts of proactive conflict resolution and structured communication and decision-making processes we were able to get back our team cohesion and maintain project momentum.
learning: By facilitating open dialogue and establishing a democratic decision-making process, I learned the importance of inclusive and structured communication in managing collaborative projects. Setting clear objectives and standards from the beginning proved crucial in aligning the team and maintaining consistent quality. However, while the project’s outcome was positive, the initial conflicts highlighted areas for improvement in project management and team alignment. In future projects, I will implement clear communication channels and decision-making processes from the outset. I will prioritize early identification and resolution of conflicts to prevent escalation. Setting explicit objectives and coding standards at the beginning will be standard practice to ensure consistency and quality. Additionally, I will foster an inclusive environment where all team members feel heard and valued, encouraging open dialogue and collaboration from the start. By applying these insights, I aim to enhance team dynamics and project outcomes in future endeavors.

pfr: Initially when receiving the task there was an air of confusion from everyone in the group which led to a detachment from everyone in the group to the task at hand which made me quite anxious that we weren’t going to be able to progress well with the Tea Making project. learning: From this experience, I learned firsthand the importance of leadership within a group environment as without leadership it, it is very hard for a group to be on the same page. situation: During the ENGG2050 course, our team was tasked with designing a smart tea maker. task_action: Our main challenge was to develop a user-friendly, efficient, and reliable tea maker that could cater to different user preferences. learning: This project has reinforced the value of critical thinking in engineering. However, we realized that the video included in the demonstration was a copyrighted lecture from another institution, which we hadn't obtained permission to use publicly in our class presentation.
task_action: As the project leader, I knew the importance of addressing this copyright issue to be at par with ethical standards in our project. I organized a meeting with the team to discuss the potential copyright infringement and its implications. We decided to contact the copyright holder for permission to use the video or find an alternative that was freely available. I took responsibility for communicating with the copyright holder while also leading the team in researching open-source educational videos that could be used as a substitute.
result: The copyright holder did not grant permission to use their video, so we opted for an open-source alternative that fit the educational theme of our project. This switch not only resolved the copyright issue but also emphasized the importance of ethical considerations in the use of digital content. Our project was successfully presented with the new video, and it was well-received by our peers and professors. This experience reinforced the importance of adhering to ethical and legal standards in software engineering and highlighted the necessity of proactive problem-solving and ethical awareness in academic and professional settings.
pfr: When I realized that our Rube Goldberg machine project had used a copyrighted video, I was first really concerned. I hadn't quite expected this task to involve such a sense of urgency and responsibility, but the realization that we might be violating intellectual property rights did. This encounter served as a sharp reminder of how our classroom efforts affect real-world situations. Even though confronting this problem was daunting, the process of finding a solution offered a practical educational opportunity. I gained a greater grasp of the ethical and collaborative aspects of engineering projects by having an honest conversation about this with my team and planning our future steps.
learning: My understanding of ethical issues in software engineering, particularly those pertaining to copyright and intellectual property, has been significantly impacted by this experience. I discovered how crucial it is to confirm the ownership and permissions to use any digital material before using it in a project, no matter how small. This is an important point that is sometimes missed in the zeal of invention and creativity. I intend to continue advocating for and upholding diligence and openness in all facets of project work going forward. Our first goal will be to make sure that all of the parts we use—hardware, software, and intellectual property—are sourced and used responsibly. situation: We defined functional units for the functionalities listed the prior week.
task_action: In out SGTA we worked together to develop categories of the machine based on the functionalities of the Tea Maker that we had listed. We had grouped them into the functional units such as power supply, ingredient storage, plumbing, mixing/heating, dispensing, computing. The functionalities listed were placed into a table under these categories of functional units to demonstrate clearly what each functional unit is responsible for in the machine.
result: we were left with a table that allowed us to understand the machine as a system made up of individual units. The units each had one or more functionalities that were required by the customer. This allows the machine to be understood clearer with components sharing functionalities being grouped into the same parts, allowing the next stage of focusing on construction and interfacing.
pfr: I found this part of the learning to be interesting as it is practicing a topic that is abstract and can be used across many fields; here we were using the skill in a particular field to focus on tangible engineering, but the idea of functional units is a topic that can be used to understand any system. The task of forming the categories for the functional unit was interesting too as it was open-ended and allowed me the freedom to make my own interpretation of how the functionalities can be compartmentalized. It was also an enlightening experience to hear what my peers had to say for their own structure of categorizing functionalities as this introduced me to other ways of viewing the same thing.
learning: This task was important for a skill that can be applied to the design of any system. This is also a cerebral skill to practice as it requires fitting the functionalities into clear categories while minimizing overlap. It also is relevant to decision-making as decisions must be made about which functional unit definitions are useful/irrelevant and which functionalities belong to which unit. I learned also about how multiple interpretations of the same task can arise and how this is useful for designing functional units that are robust as many interpretations tend to bring about deductions from the functionality that will be more accurate than a single interpretation.

situation: We needed to brainstorm ways in which our design would appeal to younger generations.
task_action: We underwent a brainstorming session in which we listed features that we would want the machine to have (Easy to clean, internet/phone, cost). We then formed our ideas into a numbered list from the most attractive features to less attractive features for young adult consumers.
result: The result was forming the basis of our design from the ideas shared in the brainstorming session by agreeing on features that our design must have to appeal to the values of young adults as well as considering how to make it affordable to that demographic of people.

situation: Needed to innovate a design for butter to be able to be dispensed into a cup in the Internet of Tea Maker.
task_action: Used a brainstorming session to evaluate the most amount of ideas possible, whether they be seemingly crazy or not. This session involved around 5-6 people where we were just saying all our ideas and writing them down. learning: By being comfortable speaking up in a group where I didn't know anyone, the design and innovation processes were able to be expedited and sped up. As I did more research and reflected on the information provided in the case study I started to understand there is almost never one right answer to a problem. To fulfil the roles and responsibilities of being an engineering requires brainstorming, teamwork, testing, re-testing and constant re-evaluation of the system and how it affects the surrounding environment. situation: I was attempting to build a DM Screen for Dungeons and Dragons with a friend of mine. We were attempting to build this screen with a lot of special requirements, such as magnetic back panels to attach notes and a large screen out of the front to display images/information.
task_action: Me and my friend underwent a brainstorming session; where we designed how each panel would sit and work. We created detailed design plans, but had an argument about how these panels should connect. I wanted these panels to connect via magnets, allowing for the ability for these panels to connect to a large tower or another panel instead. The large tower would either be a storage tower, or a dice tower. My friend wanted the panels to be in fixed positions, using hooks instead to connect the panels just to each other in a fixed order.
result: We worked out why each of us wanted this, and discussed the pros and cons of each method. We drew up two different designs, before settling on a design in the middle, where we would use a board with magnets on to allow the DM screen to connect to the magnets. Which screens/boards were placed on the board would be modular, while the positions of those screens/boards would be fixed.
pfr: When discussing each of these beliefs, we were originally both very stubborn as there were both pros and cons to each design and neither of us wanted to compromise. But as we got further into our conversation, and took a step back before looking and really listening to the points of the other person, as well as the pros and cons, we began to really see the merits of each design. By doing this, we were able to come to a compromise on the design, choosing something that kept the best aspects of both builds.
learning: By approaching this situation with the mindset of compromise, conflict resolution and taking a step back, me and my friend were able to vastly expedite the process of designing this DM screen. We were able to create more coherent and superior arguments for why each potential design would work better, and what might be flawed about our or the other person's design. The biggest piece of learning I took from this, is by taking a step back and looking at the pros of each design, we were able to come up with a design that combines the best aspects of both designs. Through this experience, I have come away with a better appreciation of conflict resolution and compromise, and a better understanding of how to handle disputes or arguments in the future.

situation: We needed to brainstorm and think creatively to achieve a proper design functionally for the internet teapot.

situation: We needed to brainstorm a design that would meet the major wants of the customer. Then communicate these ideas with other people at the table to establish the best design for the customer.
task_action: Individually we wrote down/drew ideas of how we would accomplish both the major and minor wants. We then discussed/evaluated each other's ideas/concepts, providing feedback both negative and positive to eventually establish what we as a group thought would be the best design to meet the major and minor wants of the customer.
result: This left us with a highly refined design concept, that collaterally we all agreed would be the best solution to the customer's request. situation: The task we were undertaking was developing the design for the Internet of Teas System for a customer who had very rigorous and specific demands for the way they wanted the system to behave. With such extreme and somewhat confusing demands, as a team, and independently, we had to think critically in order to meet the customer's demands. Tasks: It was our responsibility to design a system that met all of the customer's requirements even when they were confusing and sometimes very hard to cater to. For example, the customer wanted the tea maker to have tea prepared every morning when he woke up, but did not want an alarm clock system as they 'don't have an alarm clock' and 'didn't want to be spied upon,' however, they also liked the idea of customising their tea 'when setting their alarm'. This was very difficult as in order to have a system that worked according to a schedule, it would generally use an alarm clock system and it seemed the customer themself was unsure of their requirement.
task_action: In order to overcome such demanding requirements, we had to think critically. With so many precise demands, we had to break down each requirement, come up with solutions and discard them based on the other demands. Critical thinking also led us to ask critical questions, and think of solutions that may not be conventional in order to satisfy the customer.
result: Thinking critically, we asked questions regarding the scheduling of the tea maker, like whether the customer would want to set their tea each time, to which they answered that they can use the app to say when they will be getting home to set the time for tea. This seems to be an unconventional demand as it adds extra responsibility on the customer, however, it does allow us to think critically to offer solutions, despite how unique it may be. This also taught me that thinking critically is important in gathering requirements from the customer because often they themselves may not know what kind of system they want. So it is the responsibility of the engineer to ask critical questions that help the customer and developer create a clear outline of a functioning system.
pfr: Initially, the long list of demands, the contradictory and unconventional requirements was very frustrating to work with. When we thought we had come up with a solution, we would read on and find a demand that opposes the solution we came up with. This caused us to brainstorm multiple ideas but even then, it seemed as nothing would satisfy the customer. Therefore the task of meeting these requirements was extremely difficult. However, after being pushed to think critically, I have developed a greater appreciation for tasks that require you to think outside the box.
learning: Although it was initially a tiresome experience, taking a step back from thinking of conventional and straightforward solutions, I found that I had opened my eyes to a wider range of options. situation: During discussions about the Internet of Tea machine, our group had two major opposing ideas of how the tea brewing aspect of the machine will be implemented. task_action: As this divided the group into two, we needed to come up with a solution that satisfied both groups and prioritise the customer requirements. After detailed discussions, we agreed on a combined system that uses both these methods. The tea will be brewed in water, but included other features such as temperature control and separated brewing with a permeable and movable tea leaves container to help control brew time.
result: This compromise resulted in a balanced solution, that provided flexibility for the user to brew different types of tea without requiring the more advanced subsystems that would increase complexity, reduce reliability and increase design efforts and required time.
pfr: Initially, the division between the team members over the brewing methods was overwhelming as both sides presented ideas that would require two different paths to be taken in the later processes of design. situation: In one of my core mechanical engineering courses, our class was faced with the challenge of designing a cost-effective and efficient water filtration system for rural communities as part of our final year project. task_action: My role in this project was to lead the research and design phase. I conducted extensive research on existing water filtration technologies and their adaptability to rural settings. I was responsible for the prototype design, ensuring it was simple yet effective. We built and tested multiple prototypes, adjusting the proportions of sand and charcoal and experimenting with different container materials to find the most cost-effective solution.
result: The final design we developed was both affordable and efficient, successfully removing over 98% of contaminants from the water during testing phases. We presented our project at the university's engineering showcase, where it received positive feedback for its practical application and sustainability. pfr: At the beginning, I felt a potent mix of excitement and nervousness. The impact that our project could have—providing clean water to underserved populations—was incredibly motivating. Yet, the weight of leading the project's critical research and design phases sometimes felt overwhelming. As we progressed and overcame various challenges, each success boosted my confidence and deepened my commitment to the project. The positive feedback during our prototype tests was particularly affirming and fueled my enthusiasm. REFLECTION: On reflection, I realize the success of our project was significantly anchored in our initial efforts to thoroughly understand the community's needs and to set clear, realistic goals. Diving deep into the needs assessment early on set a solid foundation for our design process. It directed our efforts and allowed us to create goals that were not only specific but also achievable within our resources and time constraints.
learning: This experience taught me the critical role of conducting a detailed needs assessment at the start of any project. Understanding the specific circumstances and limitations of the end users is crucial before moving into problem-solving mode. Setting precise and measurable goals early also proved invaluable in guiding our team's efforts and maintaining focus throughout the project timeline. FUTURE ACTIONS: In future projects, I plan to dedicate more time and resources to the needs assessment phase and engage more directly with the stakeholders involved. This will ensure that the project goals are tightly aligned with the actual needs of the users. Moreover, I aim to adopt a more flexible approach to project management, allowing for iterative feedback and adjustments to our plans based on real-world testing and stakeholder input. This reflection process has not only helped me appreciate the technical skills I've developed but also underscored the importance of empathy, stakeholder engagement, and adaptive project management in engineering. These insights will undoubtedly influence how I approach future engineering challenges, making me not just a better engineer, but a more responsive and responsible one as well.

situation: I was working with one other student (semi-random) and a lecturer to research how adding tariffs to the electric chargers at Macquarie Uni has changed consumer behaviours. This had to include customer feedback, data analysis and suggested solutions, compiled into a research paper.
task_action: We obtained the data (how much power the chargers need, who charged their car and for how long, etc.) from the website that holds information on each charger you have installed for a particular party. We also created a survey for the drivers to use but we didn't get many responses at first because it was released during the holidays. This led us to extending how long it would be open for and we doubled the responses in the following month. We also had to combine our brainstormed ideas and suggestions from the public, in the survey, to come up with solutions for problems that the consumers had revealed.
result: As a result, we had a heap of compiled data on how people are using these chargers (grouping things like car models, how much revenue we are making and which locations they use to charge the most often), as well as what issues people have with the current chargers (such as the one perpetually broken charger, sun heat rendering all of them useless in the middle of the day and far away charger locations). We were then able to find new solutions and now have changed companies to people who actually help us fix the chargers and added new chargers on the other side of campus (near 4RPD/the hospital) and have potential other locations, which will hopefully please the people using them.
pfr: At first, we didn't know where or how to start, but we were led by a supervisor who gave us the relevant data and a good jumping off point. We would break down the tasks for each week/fortnight before meeting up again to catch up on what each person had completed and let the others know if we needed any help. I also gained momentum and got very invested in what we were doing as it became more interesting the deeper I went. I also felt encouraged by the positive feedback about the survey itself when a couple of people expressed in the "final comments" section that they were glad people were taking initiative to improve the charging experience at Macquarie Uni.
learning: I was able to experience frequent accountability meetings which helped me keep up with my work and have other people to lean on. I also enjoyed all the background information I learnt about electric vehicles, their chargers, and their use at this uni. I could adapt to customer feedback and use problem solving skills to find the best ways of communicating with consumers (put QR code in more places, ask people in person for general information, and convince friends to do an EV charging company for ENGG3050 presentation).

task_action: We began by assessing the needs of the community and identifying key stakeholders. We then formed subcommittees to handle different aspects of the event, such as logistics, marketing, and programming. As the team leader, I ensured that each member understood their role and responsibilities clearly. During our planning meetings, I facilitated open discussions to generate ideas and solutions. result: The outreach event was a success, with a large turnout from the community. We were able to educate people about sustainable practices through interactive workshops and demonstrations. Feedback from attendees was overwhelmingly positive, with many expressing interest in participating in future initiatives. learning: This experience taught me the importance of effective teamwork and communication in achieving common goals. Additionally, I learned the value of adaptability and flexibility when faced with unexpected obstacles, as it allowed us to navigate challenges and ultimately achieve our objectives.

situation: I was in my training as a Divemaster, and was buddied up with someone who had a bad leg.
task_action: We had to keep up with our instructor, since we we're all in a group, but my buddy could not keep up due to the problems with his leg. I eventually tried to get the person to go faster, not taking into account his situation and problems he was facing. As I realised this, I came up with an alternative course of action and surfaced instead.
result: Me and my buddy went on our own dive, with my instructor entrusting me to take care of him.
pfr: During the dive I experienced a lot of frustration and pressure. I was so primarily focused on staying close too the instructor and group, that I didn't consider my buddy's condition or situation. When we began to lag behind, I attempted to start swimming faster with my buddy, before becoming frustrated. At first with him, and then with myself. As I realised that I wasn't taking into account his condition, I stopped our swim and signalled for us to surface. I experienced a surge of empathy and accountability, and apologised for not taking into account his situation. Deciding to surface initially seemed like a failure, but I eventually realised it was a chance to make sure my partner was safe and content. In doing this, me and my instructor came up with an alternative plan of us diving separately, in a much more relaxed environment. In this, we were not only able to achieve the training goals, but also do so in a relaxed manner that accommodated his requirements. This choice resulted a more profound comprehension of the significance of leading with empathy.
learning: From this experience, I learned the profound importance of empathy and adaptability in leadership. It is clear that effective leadership is not solely about achieving goals but also about being attuned to the individual needs of team members. Pushing my buddy to keep up without considering his physical limitations was a mistake that could have been avoided by initially assessing his condition more thoroughly. This situation taught me that empathy involves actively listening and understanding others' challenges, and leadership requires flexibility to adapt plans according. In the future, I will always make sure to listen more closely to a buddy's concerns, conditions, needs or wants while ensuring that I not just hear what they say, but understand what they mean.

learning: Approaching the task from a communication standpoint, rather than a purely technical one, allowed me to become a more collaborative and understanding team member. It also helped me gain confidence in my own opinions. This experience strengthened my resolve and taught me the importance of being receptive to others' ideas. By improving my communication skills, I became easier to work with and more open to different perspectives, ultimately enhancing my effectiveness in a team environment.

situation: The project was part of a course assignment where we were tasked with developing a web application that could serve as a resource management tool for small businesses. situation: In a recent project for my ELCT4004 Power Systems Analysis, we were tasked with designing a relay system for an IEEE 14 bus system.
task_action: To accomplish this, we organized a brainstorming session with a clear mission-driven focus. A small working group was formed with a well-defined problem statement. Using the gallery method of brainstorming, each member contributed several ideas for potential relay system designs. We then evaluated and ranked the proposed solutions based on parameters such as reliability, efficiency, and ease of implementation.
result: The brainstorming session resulted in six viable relay system designs. Through a systematic evaluation process, we selected the most suitable design. Each group member was then assigned specific tasks to further develop and refine the chosen relay system.
pfr: The initial task was daunting because, as a group, it seemed the question at hand was overwhelming and that there were no optimal answers. However, as we delved into the problem systematically and documented the group decisions at each stage, we were able to reach a consensus on the design. The chosen design was based on merits that were agreed to be most important for the ascribed problem statement.
learning: By approaching decision-making using a merit-based approach and maintaining good team organization, we could expedite the decision-making process for even the most complex problems. The experience of selecting the appropriate design was dependent on the constraints and requirements, demonstrating that the notion of the “best design” is relative; every design is created for a purpose within certain limitations. Through this experience, I have come to appreciate the impact of robust and structured decision-making.

Engaging with diverse medical professionals and IT specialists, and navigating through their various expectations and visions for the project, presented a significant challenge

It highlighted the need for continuous learning and adaptation, especially when working with rapidly evolving technologies like AI in dynamic environments such as healthcare. situation: As part of our mechanical design 2 unit, our team was tasked with creating a custom-designed gearbox for use on the moon as part of a larger moon crane system.
task_action: Given the design parameters and limitations, our team must compromise on some lower-priority attributes. In order to maximise our possible score in the competition, we employed a house of quality matrix and determined the relationship between the customer requirements and the required parts and manufacturing to achieve those TPMs. From that information, we determined given the existing infrastructure the customers efficiency requirement could not be met and this was promptly communicated to the customer.
result: The customer returned to us with an updated TPM requirement, from there we devised a conceptual design and began the process of sourcing and work on our detailed design.
pfr: I felt a sense of determination and willingness to investigate all possible scenarios and compromises we had to make to ensure our design had the best chance of winning the competition. Initially, I was confused after reading our guidelines and contrasting them with the existing infrastructure technical documentation. However, after some discussion and email back and forth, I was relieved that the customer understood their oversight and adjusted their requirements. I believe this endeavour built a sense of trustworthiness and diligence with the customer and reinforced our relationship.
learning: From this experience, I learnt by taking the time to look into the details of a project you can often provide feedback for points of concern and in doing so reinforce your professional appearance towards the customer. As a result, customers might consult you for other aspects of the projects and could positively impact your professional career.

situation: We needed to undergo an innovative process in the creation of the automated safe.
task_action: The process began with the generation of an idea. The idea was to differentiate the safe from other models that were created out of metal. The safe was designed to integrate seamlessly into any household, making it indistinguishable from other items. It was to include fingerprint and PIN code locking systems for security. After the idea came the preparation, which involved drawing up designs for the safe and its dimensions, and outlining where each component would fit. Before assembling the safe, all mechanical components were tested to ensure they functioned perfectly without any issues. This led to the development stage, which involved placing each component inside the box, securing them in place, and ensuring that all components worked correctly. After assembly, the safe was tested multiple times in various environments and scenarios to ensure its full effectiveness.
result: The result was a highly innovative safe that seamlessly blended into household environments, making it indistinguishable from other items.
pfr: In the journey of conceptualizing and developing a machine to address the problem of keeping items safe, my initial reaction was a blend of excitement. The freedom to innovate without constraints was thrilling, yet the responsibility to identify a significant problem and devise a practical solution was daunting. My eagerness to embark on this creative endeavour was coupled with a sense of uncertainty about where to begin and how to navigate the complexities of design and functionality. Personal feelings played a significant role throughout this process. The initial excitement was a driving force that motivated me to dive into research and explore various problems that could be addressed through technological innovation. However, this excitement was soon tempered by the realization of the challenge ahead. The task of not just identifying a problem but also conceptualizing a machine capable of solving it was overwhelming. The transition from an abstract idea to a tangible solution required a level of creativity and problem-solving skills that I found both intimidating and invigorating. As I delved deeper into the project, the overwhelming feelings began to subside, thanks in part to the innovative processes that guided the development of the machine. These processes served as a roadmap, providing clarity and structure in uncertainty. By breaking down the project into manageable steps and focusing on each aspect of the machine's design and functionality, I was able to gradually build confidence in my ability to bring my vision to life.
learning: The learning experience from this project was profound. I gained valuable insights into the importance of a methodical approach to innovation. The realization that creativity can be channelled and structured through specific processes was enlightening. It highlighted the balance between freedom and discipline in the creative process, teaching me that innovation requires not just imagination but also a systematic approach to problem-solving.

situation: We needed to complete a report on the design and creation of a marble machine.

situation: A software engineering team was struggling with delays and inefficiencies in the deployment process.

situation: In my ENGG2000 university course, my motions team struggled to maintain individual accountability after the success of our Scoping Document.
task_action: When starting the next document, the Design document, my team allocated different sections for individuals to complete. However, people lost motivation to complete the document, and to a low standard, when other assignments and classes required more attention. learning: Through the experience of having team members who do not apply themselves to an acceptable level, I have learned to set expectations and responsibilities early on in group work. Setting up methods of holding accountability is also a priority through this experience.

situation: We needed to brainstorm methods where we can meet the design criteria for the marble machine.

task_action: Understanding the significance of being accountable, I proactively took steps to address the delay. result: Due to these measures, we witnessed substantial enhancements in the efficiency and productivity of our team. The experience highlighted the importance of being proactive in solving problems and having strong communication skills to ensure the success of a project.
learning: This experience has highlighted the significance of proactively taking charge and promoting effective communication within group environments. In the future, I will maintain a focus on proactive problem-solving and effective communication, understanding their importance in overcoming obstacles and meeting project goals. I have gained a deep understanding of the importance of accountability and teamwork in achieving project success, and I will carry these lessons with me into future collaborative projects.

situation: We must assemble and prepare the finished product for shipment by the due date.

Being held accountable helps us not break rules, and to make sure that we are doing what is necessary for the team and for what is expected from us.

result: We all downloaded discord and kept up to date with our assignment. We were able to have effective communication on how we should handle this assignment and we ended up doing good together in the assignment both academically and socially.

learning: By getting our group members on one platform we were able to have strong and effective communication as well as able to assist each other in the task we were given. learning: A clear and organised system of leadership and communication is vital for any decision making process even at the very beginning of a project and ensuring that every team members opinion is valued and considered is key for the team to be able to work together without any tension or resentment.
